newsitem.title: UK: Major blames IRA for British Grand National alert.
newsitem.headline: Major blames IRA for British Grand National alert.

text.p: The Grand National horse race, one of Britain's greatest sporting events, had to be abandoned on Saturday because of a bomb alert blamed by Prime Minister John Major on the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

The Aintree course near the north-western city of Liverpool was evacuated some 30 minutes before the scheduled start of the race after police said they had received two coded warnings of bombs at the site.
Officials later abandoned racing for the rest of the day. Security forces carried out a controlled explosion at the course after finding several suspect packages.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the alerts but Major issued a swift statement condemning the IRA as "cynical and detestable".

"I am appalled that the IRA seem to be threatening hundreds of thousands of people and causing such disruption. This is further demonstration of their contempt and disregard for the lives and interest of ordinary people," Major said.
"The IRA's campaign is cynical and detestable. They must know that this can only harden our resolve never to make concessions to terrorists," he added.

The bomb alert which stopped the 150th running of the world's most famous steeplechase followed massive disruption on motorways in central England on Thursday after the discovery of two IRA bombs on road bridges.

Aintree spokesman Nigel Payne told reporters on Saturday; "The police have received two coded bomb warnings, and they felt it was the most appropriate thing to evacuate the entire racecourse. From our point of view the safety of spectators is the most paramount thing."
Jockey Carl Llewellyn, due to ride Camelot King in the big race, described the situation as sick. "Whoever did this are not sportsmen," he said.
Jenny Pitman, trainer of such past winners as Corbieres and Royal Athlete, called for the horses to be returned to the starting gate and the race to be run.
"We cannot be held to ransom and give in to these people. We have the lunatic element here. We can't give in to them," she said.

Security sources believe the IRA, which wants an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, is trying to force Northern Ireland on to the political agenda of the British May 1 election campaign, where it has received scant attention.

IRA strategy for years has been to attack the British mainland to force British public opinion to put pressure on government to find a solution to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict, which has cost billions and 3,200 lives.
Four years ago the Grand National ended in turmoil in different circumstances after two false starts led to the race being declared void.
